we considered adding predicate but it doesn't help performance and predicates tend to constrain llvm and ptxas compiler and generate worse code quality so I don't think we want to change that part

> [...] differences in accumulation order because of the butterfly shuffle lead to the threads computing slightly different results [...] That doesn't sound right because the canonical butterfly shuffle dance guarantees bitwise-identical results in every thread, provided that the reduction operator is commutative (and IEEE-754 addition certainly is). I think that the culprit in this case is that Triton replaces one of the additions with a FMA in the final SASS: That is, after the first `SHFL.BFLY`, instead of adding the fetched squared value from the peer thread directly to our local squared value, we implicitly recalculate the local squared value by doing `fma(original_value, original_value, fetched_squared_value)`. `fma(x, x, y*y)` is not necessarily the same as `fma(y, y, x*x)`, so the commutativity assumption breaks and we get numerical differences. To be honest, I don't really understand why a FMA is needed here. In fact, the LLIR of the kernel uses regular additions everywhere, and the FMA is only introduced when lowering to PTX (and eventually SASS): ``` %11 = fmul float %10, %10, !dbg !12 ... %13 = tail call i32 @llvm.nvvm.shfl.sync.bfly.i32(i32 -1, i32 %12, i32 8, i32 31), !dbg !13 ... %15 = fadd float %11, %14, !dbg !18 ... %17 = tail call i32 @llvm.nvvm.shfl.sync.bfly.i32(i32 -1, i32 %16, i32 4, i32 31), !dbg !13 ... %19 = fadd float %15, %18, !dbg !18 ... %21 = tail call i32 @llvm.nvvm.shfl.sync.bfly.i32(i32 -1, i32 %20, i32 2, i32 31), !dbg !13 ... %23 = fadd float %19, %22, !dbg !18 ... %25 = tail call i32 @llvm.nvvm.shfl.sync.bfly.i32(i32 -1, i32 %24, i32 1, i32 31), !dbg !13 ... %27 = fadd float %23, %26, !dbg !18 ```
Is this still present in main? The reduction code has changed significantly in the last year

My analysis was for the latest available release (3.7.0), so I think that the original report is still valid. I can't actually reproduce the racecheck failure (it reports `0 hazards displayed (0 errors, 0 warnings)`), but that seems like a coincidence. A quick `cuda-gdb` session confirms that threads 23 and 24 indeed try to store different values to the same shared memory address, and these values match the original issue description exactly:
```
(cuda-gdb) x/i $pc
=> 0x752c717be0a0 <kernel+416>: STS [R5+UR4],R6
(cuda-gdb) cuda thread 23
...
(cuda-gdb) p $R5
$21 = 4
(cuda-gdb) p/x $R6
$22 = 0x41a81a02
(cuda-gdb) cuda thread 24
...
(cuda-gdb) p $R5
$23 = 4
```

Yep, this is still an issue, and it's the typical `fma` problem you may hit. There are a few solutions:
Fording `fma` directly
```

```
or use `enable_fp_fusion=False`.

Tried again and predicating the stores give you a 5% perf hit which is a bit annoying (but would be, at heart, the right solution).

issue.body:
### Describe the bug

When lowering a reduction followed by a layout conversion, Triton likes to generate code of the following form for intermediate warp results:

1. Threads 0-n perform a butterfly shuffle so that each thread now has the accumulated result (the sum, for example).
2. Threads 0-n all write the "same" result to the bucket in shared memory assigned to that result.

Unfortunately, while this makes sense in theory, in practice differences in accumulation order because of the butterfly shuffle lead to the threads computing slightly different results. Then, when each thread goes to write its data, this causes data races because they write different data to the same memory location. Here is a test program that demonstrates the problem:

```python3
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import torch
import triton


@triton.jit
def kernel(
	x,
	y,
	D: triton.language.constexpr,
	M: triton.language.constexpr,
	N: triton.language.constexpr,
):
	x = triton.language.make_block_ptr(
		base=x,
		shape=(M, D),
		strides=(D, 1),
		offsets=(0, 0),
		block_shape=(M, D),
		order=(1, 0),
	)

	x = triton.language.load(x)
	x = (x * x).sum(axis=1)
	x = x.expand_dims(0).broadcast_to(N, M)

	y = triton.language.make_block_ptr(
		base=y,
		shape=(N, M),
		strides=(M, 1),
		offsets=(0, 0),
		block_shape=(N, M),
		order=(1, 0),
	)

	triton.language.store(y, x)


torch.manual_seed(42)
m = 8
n = 32
d = 16
x = torch.randn((m, d), dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")
y = torch.zeros(n, m, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda")

kernel[(1,)](x, y, d, m, n)
```

With a bit of debugging, one can find that groups of 16 threads cooperate to compute the sum across their elements, and get assigned one result among them. In this case, thread 23 is trying to write 21.0126991 (0x41a81a02) to the same bucket as thread 24, which computes the result 21.012701 (0x41a81a03). This discrepancy triggers racecheck :(

I'm not entirely sure what the best solution to this is (hence why this is an issue and not a PR). One answer is we just ignore the problem since it doesn't really matter numerically–it's a "benign" race. Another is we can get a "leader" thread to write the result and the other threads can mask themselves out. This would require an extra check but perhaps it might still be a performance win by reducing shared memory traffic?

### Environment details

Triton: main
GPU: GH200
issue.title: Butterfly shuffles in reductions trigger racecheck because they are not numerically stable
